ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, under the action of a force acting on the midpoint of OP and perpendicular to OP, the conducting rod OP rotates about the O axis along a smooth semicircular frame of radius r in a uniform magnetic field with a certain angular velocity. The magnetic induction intensity of the magnetic field is B, a resistor R is connected between A and O, the resistance of the rod and the frame is neglected, and the total electric power in the circuit is P. Find the angular velocity of rotation of the conducting rod.
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The angular velocity of rotation of the conducting rod is $\frac{2\sqrt{PR}}{Br^2}$
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there is a smooth semicircular conducting frame with radius r, O is located at the center of the semicircle and at the rotation axis, and A is near the right endpoint; the conducting rod OP points from O to the point P on the semicircular track, so OP is in the radial direction and has length r. The uniform “×” in the figure indicates that the uniform magnetic field is perpendicular to the paper surface and directed inward. At the midpoint of OP there is an external force F perpendicular to the rod; a resistor R is connected between O and A, and the problem states that the resistance of the rod and the frame is neglected, so in the closed circuit only R consumes electric power. Then reason: When the conducting rod rotates about O with angular velocity ω, the speed of a small element on the rod at a distance x from O is v=ωx, and the direction is perpendicular to the rod. The motional electromotive force produced by this small element is dε=Bv dx=Bωx dx. Integrating along the whole rod from x=0 to x=r gives ε=∫_0^r Bωx dx=(1/2)Bωr^2. The total resistance of the circuit is R, and the total electric power in the circuit is P=ε^2/R, therefore P=[(1/2)Bωr^2]^2/R=B^2ω^2r^4/(4R). Solving gives the magnitude of the angular velocity ω=2√(PR)/(Br^2).
